Owner-Operators|U|Universe: Terry Smith states that leaving out utilities, telecoms, transport, energy, materials and retailing means skipping businesses whose returns stay low, because returns on capital persist for decades and being cheap doesn't turn a bad company into a good one. A mentioned example: airlines, which he says never make an adequate return on capital. Chris Hohn states that avoiding banks, autos, retail, insurance, commodities, airlines, telecoms and media means skipping businesses without real barriers to entry, because growth without barriers earns little for owners. A mentioned example: airlines grew about 5% a year for a century with minimal profit.
Owner-Operators|O1|History: Terry Smith states that a long record of returns means you can tell a truly good company from a lucky one, because high and low returns on capital tend to persist for decades. A mentioned example: return-on-equity data back to 1966, where the high-return group kept clustering around 20% and stayed well above the low group. Joel Greenblatt states that one year of high returns proves little, because last year's return on capital may be a cyclical peak or include one-off items, so it may not be the return going forward. No specific past example given.
Owner-Operators|O2|Recent report: No investor source: old filings can hide a recent collapse, so the screen only uses companies with a fresh annual report.
Owner-Operators|O3|Size (revenue): No investor source: very small filers have patchy data and are hard to own in a meaningful size.
Owner-Operators|O4|Insider ownership: Murray Stahl states that high insider ownership means an owner-operator, someone who runs the company because they own more of it than anyone else, because their wealth moves with the shares; float-weighted indexes also underweight such firms, leaving them cheaper. A mentioned example: his S&P 500 study back to 1957, where owner-operators earned the bulk of the return. Chris Davis states that managers who are real owners means incentives are aligned with shareholders, because managers who aren't owners chase the most pay possible, which is an expense for owners; "We want to invest in owner-operators." No specific past example given. Connor Haley states that management owning at least about 5% in small and micro caps means they care about shareholders, because their own net worth rises and falls with the stock. A mentioned example: XPEL's CEO Ryan Pape keeps a material part of his net worth in the stock and, Haley believes, has never sold a share.
Owner-Operators|O5|Consistent profits: Connor Haley states that a record of profits means a proven business rather than a cash burner, because companies already making money don't need to dilute shareholders to survive and can grow into operating leverage. A mentioned example: Alta Fox's study of 104 multibaggers from 2015-20, most of which were already profitable five years before their big run. Joel Greenblatt states that a single bad year should not disqualify a steady business, because what matters is normalized earnings across years: a company earning $10 for nine years and breaking even in one is worth roughly $9 of normal earnings. No specific past example given.
Owner-Operators|O6|High returns: Terry Smith states that a high return on capital means a business can compound in value, because over a long holding your return converges on what the business earns on its capital; he calls return on capital "the single most important thing". A mentioned example: airlines, which he says never make an adequate return on capital. Joel Greenblatt states that a high return on tangible capital means a good business, because it shows the profit on each dollar tied up in the business: pre-tax 14% is generally not good, while 20% (about 12% after tax) is decent. A mentioned example: Moody's, which needed no reinvestment and was the best business he had ever found.
Owner-Operators|O7|Cash conversion: Connor Haley states that relying on free cash flow means trusting the number hardest to fake, because earnings and EBITDA "can be easily manipulated". No specific past example given. Terry Smith states that good cash conversion is a mark of quality, because profits only count if they arrive as cash, so he measures return on capital in cash. A mentioned example: the MSCI World quality subset (high returns, high margins, good cash conversion) beat the index in every rolling 10-year period since 1996. Dan Sundheim states that profits that don't reconcile with the cash and unit economics can signal accounting abuse, because capitalizing costs that should be expensed lifts profit without bringing in cash. A mentioned example: Orthodontic Centers of America, where he found "the simplest form of accounting fraud".
Owner-Operators|O8|Leverage: Connor Haley states that heavy borrowing means even a well-run company can be wiped out by a shock it didn't cause, because debt leaves no time to wait for normal conditions. A mentioned example: a restaurant stock that borrowed for an acquisition just before COVID; its CEO talked of selling wine inventory for cash, so Alta Fox sold. It survived, but he defends the sale. Brian Gaines states that a heavily indebted company's shares become an option bet rather than a business you can value, because with large debt against a small equity base, "the movements in the stock price don't mean much" for the company's value. A mentioned example: Movie Gallery, with $1.1 billion of debt against 30 million shares.
Owner-Operators|O9|Size (market cap): No investor source: a minimum market value keeps out stocks too small to buy without moving the price.
Owner-Operators|O10|Liquidity: No investor source: enough daily trading is needed to get in and out without a big price impact.
Owner-Operators|O11|Valuation: Murray Stahl states that owner-operators often carry the lowest valuations, something he said shouldn't exist yet does, because float-weighted index money underweights firms with large insider stakes, so fewer buyers bid them up. A price cap therefore rarely shuts out good owner-operators. No specific past example given. Joel Greenblatt states that price should be judged as enterprise value against pre-tax operating profit (EBIT), because that compares companies fairly whatever their debt and tax; even 12x EBIT needs a pretty good business. A mentioned example: he bought Moody's at a P/E of 20, not what he would normally do, because the business was so good.
Owner-Operators|Flag|Margin collapse / r: Murray Stahl states that flat revenues, rising costs, too much debt and near-term maturities mark a bad company (from a 1985 lecture recalled by co-founder Steven Bregman), because shrinking sales and squeezed margins leave less cash to meet obligations. No specific past example given. Brian Gaines states that a sudden drop in profit per sale can mean the business economics are broken, because a dominant rival's price move can permanently cut what each sale earns. A mentioned example: when Blockbuster dropped late fees he worked out gross profit per movie falling to about $1.69, called the business "absolutely destroyed" and sold Movie Gallery. Joel Greenblatt, passing on a question Rich Pzena asks, states that a troubled stock needs one answer: is the problem temporary or permanent, because temporary problems can recover while permanent ones keep eroding value. No specific past example given.
Owner-Operators|J|Human / AI review: Murray Stahl states that an agent-operator, a manager paid in ways unrelated to the long-term value of the shares, is a red flag, because such a manager can do well while shareholders don't, unlike an owner-operator. No specific past example given. Chris Davis states that long-dated pay means a management culture built for the long term, because executives can't cash in on short-term moves. A mentioned example: Exxon, whose executive pay vests 10 years after retirement, a culture he says you could see in its proxy statements for years. Connor Haley states that pay tied to stock rather than cash, and how management uses spare cash, show whether managers truly serve shareholders, because ownership alone doesn't guarantee good capital allocation. A mentioned example: Collectors Universe, Alta Fox's first activist campaign, paid out cash as dividends despite amazing reinvestment opportunities, which wasn't readily apparent in the financials.
Hard Assets & Royalties|U|Universe: Murray Stahl states that owning land, royalties, water and similar hard assets means exposure to the tangible assets the S&P 500 barely holds, because owners collect income without running or funding the operation, and it tends to rise with inflation. A mentioned example: Texas Pacific Land, which he owned from 1984, whose easement and water income grew once fracking operators had to cross its land.
Hard Assets & Royalties|R1|History: Joel Greenblatt states that judging a cyclical business needs several years of results, because last year's high return on capital could be a cyclical peak; he gives an oil company's high return last year as an illustration of a number that may not last. No specific past example given. Terry Smith states that a real grower should be bigger at each peak and each trough of the business cycle than at the previous ones, because that separates lasting growth from cyclical swings, and only several years of data can show it. No specific past example given.

Hard Assets & Royalties|R4|Little reinve: Murray Stahl states that a royalty or land company needing almost no reinvestment means shareholders truly own its earnings, because no cash must be spent to keep the income coming; he called a royalty a call option on everything. A mentioned example: Texas Pacific Land, which has no reinvestment requirement; one royalty company even held more reserves after 30 years. Joel Greenblatt states that growth needing no reinvestment means each dollar of earnings is worth more, because the owner keeps the full dollar instead of putting part back into the business. A mentioned example: Moody's reinvested nothing, while Coca-Cola had to reinvest about 20% of its earnings to grow.
Hard Assets & Royalties|R5|Royalty-like: Murray Stahl states that very high margins mean a company owns the asset rather than works it, because the royalty holder does not run the mine, so when output rises "it goes to the bottom line because it's a royalty". A mentioned example: Franco-Nevada, where two-thirds to 70% of its royalty assets produce no gold until gold prices are considerably higher.
Hard Assets & Royalties|R6|Consistent pr: Joel Greenblatt states that a business should be judged on normalized earnings across good and bad years, because one weak year says little if it earns steadily the rest of the time: $10 a year for nine years and break-even in one is roughly $9 of normal earnings. No specific past example given.
Hard Assets & Royalties|R7|Leverage: Murray Stahl states that too much debt and near-term maturities mark a bad company (from a 1985 lecture recalled by co-founder Steven Bregman), because debt has to be repaid on schedule whatever happens to revenue. No specific past example given. Sander Gerber states that heavy leverage built up when rates were low means financial structures may break, because if long-term rates stay higher, borrowers can't refinance at the same rate or make their debt payments. No specific past example given.

Hard Assets & Royalties|R10|Valuation: Murray Stahl states that a royalty company can merit a higher earnings multiple than a business that must reinvest, because its owners keep all the earnings, so other firms' P/Es should be adjusted for required reinvestment. Yet he still bought cheap. A mentioned example: in 1995 the market valued Texas Pacific Land at about $54 an acre while its land sales averaged $192. Joel Greenblatt states that even a great business that needs no reinvestment has a price limit, because the earnings yield must still clear a floor; he would "never use less than six percent". A mentioned example: he paid a P/E of 20 for Moody's, above his norm, but said he wouldn't pay 30 times earnings for most businesses.
Hard Assets & Royalties|J|Human / AI rev: Murray Stahl states that hidden assets, dependence on one commodity and the operator's choices all matter for royalty owners, because accounting can carry land at no value and a royalty's cash rides on one commodity and the operator's decisions. A mentioned example: San Juan Basin Royalty Trust, 99.8% gas, cut its payout to zero to fund operator Hilcorp's capex; Texas Pacific Land once assigned its property no value.
